title: FRM Quant, Lesson 6: Monte Carlo simulation and variance reduction
subtitle: When the problem has no closed-form solution, you generate tens of thousands of fake futures and count
whyItMatters: Monte Carlo is the universal tool of risk management: pricing complex products, computing VaR on a multi-asset portfolio, modelling operational losses. It also creates a false sense of precision very easily, because the output looks extremely specific even when the input assumptions are entirely wrong.
openingQuestion: At what rate does the standard error of a Monte Carlo estimate fall as the number of runs increases?
openingOptions: Inversely with the square root of the number of runs
Inversely with the number of runs, so doubling the runs halves the error
Exponentially, so a few hundred extra runs bring the error close to zero
It does not depend on the number of runs at all, only on the quality of the random number generator
explanation: Monte Carlo simulation generates thousands of random scenarios and draws conclusions from the distribution of outcomes, which lets it handle problems that have no analytical solution. The price is square-root convergence: halving the error means running four times as many paths, and each path may require revaluing the whole portfolio. That is why variance reduction techniques exist - they buy accuracy through design instead of through run count.

diagram.label: Specify a distribution for the input risk factors
Generate tens of thousands of random scenarios from it
Revalue the portfolio under every scenario
Aggregate the distribution of outcomes → read off the quantile you need

realWorldExample.company: The compute cost of a full-portfolio simulation
realWorldExample.description: For a large portfolio holding many complex derivatives, each scenario requires revaluing the entire book, and valuing some of those products itself needs a nested simulation inside. The compute cost grows multiplicatively, which makes variance reduction techniques and approximation methods not an optimisation for its own sake but the condition for the problem to run in any useful amount of time.

quiz.question: How does the antithetic variates technique reduce variance?
options: It drops the scenarios producing extreme results from the sample
It pairs each random path with its mirror so the errors offset
It doubles the number of runs and averages the two batches
It uses a higher quality random number generator
quiz.explanation: If one path comes out biased high, its mirror image tends to come out biased low. The average of the pair has lower variance than the average of two independent paths, so the same accuracy is reached with fewer runs. Doubling the runs would also reduce variance, but only at the square-root rate that antithetic pairing beats for free. Discarding extreme scenarios would bias the estimate rather than sharpen it, and a better generator improves the quality of the draws without changing the convergence rate at all.

quiz.question: In which situation is importance sampling especially useful?
options: When the model has fewer than three risk factors in total
When the input distribution is the standard normal one
When you need the probability of a rare event
When you need the mean of the whole result distribution
quiz.explanation: Ordinary simulation allocates effort in proportion to probability density, so most of the scenarios land in the ordinary range. Importance sampling shifts the sampling distribution toward the tail and then corrects the weights - concentrating the computation exactly where the answer is needed. For a mean over the whole distribution, plain sampling is already efficient and reweighting only adds variance. The number of factors and the shape of the input distribution decide nothing here; what decides is how rare the region of interest is.

quiz.question: What is the biggest risk in using Monte Carlo results?
options: The results cannot be reproduced because the method is random
The results always come out below the true value in every case
The simulation only runs on histories longer than twenty years
The result looks precise but rests entirely on the input assumptions
quiz.explanation: A number carried to three decimal places after a million runs feels certain, but that precision describes the simulation error only and says nothing about whether the input assumptions are right. Get the inputs wrong and the simulation merely helps you be wrong very precisely. Reproducibility is not the issue - fixing the random seed makes any run repeatable for an auditor - and there is no systematic downward bias, nor any minimum length of history: Monte Carlo can be run on assumptions with no history behind them at all.

quiz.question: In which situation is importance sampling most useful?
options: When the event being measured is so rare that plain simulation rarely reaches it
When the number of random variables in the model is too large to compute in reasonable time
When the input distribution is unknown and has to be estimated from data
When the simulation output has to be checked against a known closed-form answer
quiz.explanation: To estimate the probability of an event that happens once in ten thousand, plain simulation has to run an enormous number of paths before it registers a handful of hits. Importance sampling shifts the distribution so that many scenarios are generated in the region of interest, then corrects the weights. It does not shrink the dimension of the problem, so it is no answer to too many variables, and it presumes you know the distribution rather than helping you estimate one. Checking against a closed-form answer is what control variates do.

quiz.question: What is the biggest risk when relying on Monte Carlo output?
options: The output changes on every run, so it cannot be reproduced for the auditors
The sheer number of scenarios conveys a certainty the model does not have
The computation takes far too long to use in day-to-day decisions
The method only applies to portfolios holding a few asset classes
quiz.explanation: A hundred thousand scenarios look far more convincing than a formula, yet all of them are generated from the same set of assumptions about distributions and correlations. If those assumptions are wrong, the simulation only makes the error more detailed rather than more correct. The other candidates are engineering matters with known fixes: a fixed seed makes runs reproducible, the run count can be cut when speed matters, and the method scales to any number of asset classes - it is the assumptions that do not scale.

practicePrompt.question: Running 10,000 simulations gives a standard error of 0.4%. How many runs are needed to bring the standard error down to 0.1%?
options: 160,000 (= 10,000 × 16, because error goes as the root)
40,000 (= 10,000 × 4, in proportion to the error)
2,500 (= 10,000 / 4, fewer runs to go faster)
practicePrompt.explanation: Monte Carlo error falls with the square root of the run count, so cutting the error by a factor of 4 means multiplying the runs by 16. This square-root relationship is the reason variance reduction techniques exist: antithetic variates and importance sampling are far cheaper than buying accuracy with raw compute. And remember that the 0.1% figure only says how far the simulation has converged around the value the INPUT ASSUMPTIONS imply - it says nothing about whether those distribution and correlation assumptions are right.

keyTakeaways: Monte Carlo error falls with the square root of the run count - buying accuracy is expensive
Antithetic variates pair mirrored paths so their errors offset each other
Importance sampling shifts computational effort toward the tail and then corrects the weights
Simulation precision says nothing about whether the input assumptions are correct

summary.keyIdea: Monte Carlo solves problems that have no closed-form answer, but the quality of the result is capped by the quality of the distribution and correlation assumptions
summary.commonMistake: Mistaking a small simulation error for a correct model, which leads to over-confidence in the final number
summary.action: Always run the simulation under several different correlation assumptions to see how sensitive the result is

application.title: Simulation for a personal plan
application.message: Instead of assuming your portfolio returns exactly 8% a year, try picturing the distribution of outcomes that could occur - the worst scenario within it is what decides whether your plan can take the strain.
application.secondary: This is the spirit of simulation: do not ask for the average outcome, ask for the whole range of them.

sections.text: When a problem is too complex for a formula, what is left is to generate a great many hypothetical versions of the future and count in how many of them each thing happens.

items: Identify the risk factors together with their distributions and the correlation structure between them
Generate a large number of random scenarios following that structure
Revalue the entire portfolio under each scenario
Aggregate the distribution of outcomes and read off the quantile or expectation you need

sections.text: The standard error is inversely proportional to the square root of the run count, so halving the error means running four times as many paths. For a portfolio where a single valuation is already expensive, that cost rapidly becomes unacceptable - which is why variance reduction techniques are not an option but a precondition.

items: Antithetic variates: pair each random path with its mirror image so the errors offset
Control variates: use a closely related problem with a closed-form solution to correct the result
Importance sampling: shift the sampling distribution toward the tail and then correct the weights
Stratified sampling: divide the outcome space into strata and ensure each stratum gets enough draws

sections.label: The false sense of precision
sections.text: After ten million runs the result appears with three decimal places and looks entirely credible. But that precision describes the simulation error alone. If the input correlation matrix is wrong - and in a crisis correlations always move - the simulation only helps you be wrong very precisely.

lines: Simulation creates no new information; it only works out the consequences of the assumptions you fed it.
Next lesson: resampling techniques that need no distributional assumption at all.
